Doubtful
dout´fool
adj. (wavering; unsettled; of a mind held in suspense)
From doubt, Latin dubitare, to waver. Both New Testament uses concern a mind suspended — over food and tomorrow in Luke, over disputable matters in Romans.

Biblical Definition

Our Lord forbids a particular kind of mental suspension: “And seek not ye what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink, neither be ye of doubtful mind” (Luke 12:29). The Greek behind doubtful mind pictures a ship riding high and unsettled, and the cure He gives is not effort but knowledge of the Father: “For all these things do the nations of the world seek after: and your Father knoweth that ye have need of these things” (Luke 12:30). Paul uses the word of a different suspense — the disputed questions that divide congregations: “Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations” (Romans 14:1). The weaker brother is to be welcomed, not enrolled in an argument about his scruples. Paul then gives the rule that governs the whole chapter: “And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin” (Romans 14:23). A man must not act against his own conscience even when his conscience is poorly informed; he must have it better informed first. Two texts, two different doubts — anxiety about provision and uncertainty about liberty — and in both the answer is a settled confidence: in the Father who knows, and in the Lord to whom every servant stands or falls.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines doubtful as dubious; not settled in opinion; undetermined; wavering; hesitating.

expand to see more

DOUBTFUL, a. Dubious; not settled in opinion; undetermined; wavering; hesitating.

DOUBT, v.i. To waver or fluctuate in opinion; to hesitate; to be in suspense.

DISPUTATION, n. The act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition to something.

CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge; the faculty by which we judge of the moral rectitude of our own actions.

SCRUPLE, n. Doubt; hesitation from the difficulty of determining what is right.

Key Scripture

Luke 12:29 — "And seek not ye what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink, neither be ye of doubtful mind."

Luke 12:30 — "For all these things do the nations of the world seek after: and your Father knoweth that ye have need of these things."

Romans 14:1 — "Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations."

Romans 14:23 — "And he that doubteth is damned if he eat, because he eateth not of faith: for whatsoever is not of faith is sin."

Modern Corruption

Doubt is promoted from a condition to be cured into a virtue to be cultivated, and a chapter written to protect the weak conscience is used to make uncertainty itself the mark of an honest faith.

expand to see more

A considerable strand of modern religious writing treats doubt as the more honest posture and certainty as arrogance — faith redefined as a comfort with unanswered questions. Scripture does not flatter doubt. James says the wavering man is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed, and must not think he shall receive anything of the Lord. Our Lord treats the doubtful mind as a symptom of not knowing the Father well enough, and prescribes knowledge rather than resignation. Honest questions are everywhere in the Bible — the Psalms are full of them — but they are always addressed to God and always press toward an answer.

Romans 14 is meanwhile put to a use Paul never intended, as a general instruction to treat contested doctrines as matters of indifference. The chapter is about meat, drink and holy days — genuinely indifferent things — and its ruling principle is that a man must not violate his own conscience. Paul had no such tolerance for the Galatian error or the Corinthian denial of the resurrection; on those he was immovable. Wisdom lies in telling the two categories apart, and a church that files justification under doubtful disputations has not learned charity. It has lost the faith it was charitable about.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek meteorizomai (G3349), to be held in suspense; diakrisis dialogismon, discerning of thoughts; diakrino (G1252), to waver; asthenes (G772), weak.

expand to see more

Greek meteorizomai (G3349) — to be raised aloft, held in suspense; Luke 12:29, doubtful mind.

Greek dialogismos (G1261) — reasoning, disputing; Romans 14:1, doubtful disputations.

Greek diakrino (G1252) — to waver, be at variance with oneself; Romans 14:23, he that doubteth.

Greek astheneo (G770) — to be weak; him that is weak in the faith.

Greek pistis (G4102) — faith; whatsoever is not of faith is sin.

Usage

"“Neither be ye of doubtful mind” — the suspense our Lord forbids."

"“Not to doubtful disputations” — how the weak brother is received."

"“Whatsoever is not of faith is sin” — the rule for a scrupled conscience."
